name: Kim Maida
bio: Kim is the Head of Developer Relations and Founding GTM Engineer working on security for agents at Keycard. Kim's career is rooted in Identity, software engineering, and developer experience strategy. She enjoys teaching, mentoring, and learning from folks in the product technology space and loves to travel, overland, design stickers, and craft miniatures and artisan keycaps.

positions.claim: Giving agents long-lived API keys makes them overprivileged and lets them act on decisions the user may not agree with, even under supervision.
Human-in-the-loop approval alone is not a sufficient access control, because humans are consent-fatigued and make mistakes, and many agents run autonomously anyway.
An agent will use every permission it has access to in order to complete a task.
Agent access control does not require a new specification; RFC 8693 token exchange, an existing OAuth 2 extension, is sufficient.
Tokens should be requested per tool call rather than per session, so the agent only receives permissions for the single action it is currently proposing.
Downstream access tokens should be audience-bound to a single target MCP server, expire within a few minutes, and never be stored.
No agent should be permitted to drop a database, even when the documented recovery procedure calls for it.
Evaluating policy before minting a credential is strictly safer than issuing a broad credential and restricting its use, because a denied action leaves nothing to leak, replay, or steal.
A human's approval of an agent action should itself be checked against policy and the approver's role, and can be overridden.
Building on open standards makes the access-control layer forward-compatible with agent frameworks and protocols that do not exist yet.
Teams defining scopes should start from the scopes their resource server already exposes, then layer tool-call-level scopes on top or pass them through.
The right place to enforce access control is between the runtime and the MCP server, at the point the token is requested, rather than only at the resource.
